Dear Jaya,

You asked how the first club meeting of the year went, so here is the honest version. Last year I noticed the loudest three people always decided everything, so this time I handed out slips and said: five minutes, total silence, write anything. It felt strange. Nobody looked at anybody. Then we read the slips aloud with no names. Tashi, who has hardly spoken since joining in July, had written: a quiz round where teams pick their own topics. Half the room said yes at once. I had been nervous the meeting would drag, but it ended early and we chose that quiz. I think I will keep the silent five minutes.

Dolma

Simran, you asked how our quiz club picked the inter-school event format. So here's the story from me, Sonali, club captain.
Last year, meetings were always the same. Three loud seniors spoke first, everyone else nodded, and we did what the seniors wanted.
This time I thought, the first idea spoken always wins, not the best one. So I handed out slips and said, "Five minutes, write your ideas alone. No talking."
Then I read the slips aloud without names. There were eleven ideas. Most were the usual buzzer round. But one slip said: "Teams build their own questions for the other team, and we judge the questions too."
Everyone loved it. After the vote, I asked who wrote it. Rekha from Class 9, who has never spoken in a meeting, raised her hand very slowly.
That's our format now.

qa.q: How many ideas were on the slips?
How do you think Rekha felt when she raised her hand very slowly?
qa.a: She was probably shy and nervous, but also proud that her idea was chosen.

qa.q: Why did writing alone first work better than open discussion?
qa.a: Because the loud seniors couldn't set the direction first, so quieter members like Rekha could share ideas without being drowned out.

qa.q: How might the three loud seniors see the new way of choosing?
qa.a: They may feel a little sidelined at first, but could also see that the club found a better idea than the usual buzzer round.

grounding: It shows a club captain asking members to write ideas silently before discussion, so a shy member's quiz format becomes the choice.

I'm Vinita, I'm in the science club, and I noticed something at Tuesday's meeting that I keep thinking about.
Lokesh, our captain, didn't let anyone speak at the start. He gave each of us a sticky note and said, "Five minutes, write your idea for our open day event. Alone."
Usually Aryan talks first and we all go along. This time the room was silent except for pens.
Then Lokesh stuck all the notes on the board. Some were poster shows, some a magic-science demo. One note said: "A quiz where visitors play against club members, with torches as buzzers."
It was from Meera, who never talks in meetings.
When the class voted, the torch quiz won by a lot. Meera was looking down at her desk, but she was smiling. I don't know what Lokesh was thinking, but he looked very pleased.

qa.q: What did Lokesh give each member at the start?
qa.a: He gave each of us a sticky note.

qa.q: What might Meera looking down but smiling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Meera felt shy but happy and proud that the idea won, though Vinita can only guess.

qa.q: What else could Lokesh try to keep quieter members involved?
qa.a: He could keep the silent writing for every meeting and let quieter members present their own notes, if they want to.

qa.q: How might Aryan experience this new way of starting meetings?
qa.a: Aryan may feel a bit held back from speaking first, but still gets to share an idea on a note like everyone else.

grounding: It shows a captain asking members to write ideas silently before discussion, so a quiet member's suggestion becomes the choice.
